description: Create YouTube Shorts ads from one product photo: a full-screen vertical clip in 6, 10 or 15 seconds. See the cost first and start yours now.
h1: YouTube Shorts Ads Made From a Single Product Photo
lead: YouTube Shorts ads play full screen on a phone. Turn a product photo into a vertical clip that shows what the product does before the viewer moves on.
card: Full-screen vertical clips that show what your product does.
intro: YouTube Shorts sit between quick videos people chose to watch, so an ad there works when it feels like one more useful clip: a product shown clearly, doing something real. Upload a product photo, add a sentence about what should happen, and AIVideosUGC returns a 9:16 clip that fills the screen, in your choice of 6, 10 or 15 seconds. Need a wider cut for a regular YouTube video or in-stream ad? Choose 16:9 instead.

Demo-style clips suit Shorts well. Try a hand blender whirring in a glass, a backpack being packed for a trip, or a desk lamp clicking on at dusk. Each clip is made separately and shows its cost first. Add any music and on-screen text in CapCut or another editor, then upload the finished file to your YouTube channel or ad account. Use a short product demo for the 6, 10 or 15-second file, a creator face-to-camera explanation when the product needs context, and a centered frame with open space when you will add captions later. The generated image or clip has no baked-in words.

faq.q: Can I use my TikTok video as a YouTube Short?
faq.a: Yes, the same 9:16 file works on both. Watch it in the Shorts player before you run it, to make sure nothing important hides under the buttons.

faq.q: Can I add sound to my Shorts ad?
faq.a: Yes, after download. Add music in CapCut or another editor, or pick audio inside YouTube, before the clip goes live. We don't add sound ourselves.

faq.q: Is a 6-second clip long enough for a Shorts ad?
faq.a: For one clear product moment, six seconds can work. Ten or fifteen seconds leaves more room for a demonstration from start to finish.

faq.q: What are YouTube Shorts ad limits?
faq.a: Square or vertical uploads up to 3 minutes can qualify as Shorts. Google Ads Shorts video ads can also run up to 3 minutes; AIVideosUGC offers 6, 10 or 15-second jobs. See [YouTube upload guidance](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/15424877) and [Google Ads Shorts specs](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/16041697?hl=en).

faq.q: What should appear in the first second of a Short?
faq.a: Show the product and the start of one action immediately, then let the clip finish that action without relying on a title card or spoken explanation.

faq.q: When should I use 16:9 instead of Shorts?
faq.a: Use 16:9 for a regular YouTube video or in-stream placement. It is a separate wide output and should not be labeled as a Shorts format.

overview.h2: Give a Short one clear product beat
overview.d: A Short works best when the viewer can understand the object and the action without waiting for a spoken narration. Start from a photo that shows the working parts, then describe a beginning, one movement, and a finish: the lid opens, the contents appear, and the product settles into use. That sequence also gives the clip a natural point to loop.

overview.h2: Use Google's guidance as the publishing check
overview.d: YouTube Help says square or vertical uploads can qualify as Shorts up to 3 minutes. Google Ads recommends 9:16 creative at 1080×1920 for Shorts ads. AIVideosUGC offers 6, 10, and 15 second jobs; its five generator shapes are 9:16, 1:1, 16:9, 4:3, and 3:4. Choose 16:9 for a standard YouTube video or in-stream ad, not for a Shorts card. Read [YouTube's Shorts upload guidance](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/15424877) and [Google Ads Demand Gen video specs](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/17140777?hl=en) before publishing.

overview.h2: Start with the action viewers came to see
overview.d: A Short should make the object and its change clear immediately. Describe the starting position, one movement, and the final hold: a steamer smooths one shirt panel, a speaker button is pressed, or a snack pouch opens before the first bite. Keep the subject centered enough for the Shorts feed while leaving edge room for controls and captions.

overview.h2: Know when the wide cut belongs elsewhere
overview.d: Use the 9:16 output for the Shorts feed and make a separate 16:9 job for a standard YouTube video or in-stream placement. Do not stretch a vertical frame into a wide player. The same product story can carry across both files, but rewrite the camera direction so the product remains large and complete in each crop.

overview.h2: Add the publish details after export
overview.d: Download the clip, review the opening and final frame, then add music, captions, product links, and the description in YouTube Studio or your ad account. Check current upload duration and orientation guidance at publishing time. Keep health, performance, or comparison claims supported by your own product information before the file goes live.

overview.h2: Plan the Shorts frame before the edit
overview.d: Choose one hands-on demo for a 15-second-ready Shorts cut, a creator face-to-camera review, or a centered product frame with open subtitle space. AIVideosUGC supplies the visual starting point in 6, 10 or 15 seconds; add narration, captions and music in your editor, then check the vertical preview.

input_guide.h2: Photograph the parts that need to move

items.d: Show the lid, hinge, nozzle, zipper, switch, or handle that the scene will use. The source image should give that part enough room to move.
Write what is visible first, what happens next, and where the action ends. This keeps a short clip from trying to tell three stories.
Place the product where the title, channel controls, and buttons are less likely to cover it; add any exact text after download.

results.h2: A Short that can stand on its own

items.d: The product should be visible before the movement begins, so the viewer knows what the clip is showing.
Show a single use or reveal from start to finish instead of relying on a title card.
End close to the opening position when the action naturally repeats, or use a decisive final frame so the product stays easy to recognize.
A travel backpack receives one folded shirt, the zipper closes, and a hand lifts it from a bench.
A blender cup receives frozen fruit, the blade turns briefly, and the finished drink appears in a clear glass.
A desk lamp clicks on beside a notebook as the room changes from evening shade to a warm pool of light.
A plain box opens, the product is lifted into the center, and one key component is shown close to the camera.

after_download.h2: Finish the Short in your publishing tools

items.d: Type the product name, price, offer, and any required disclosure yourself so the words are accurate.
Select audio in YouTube, CapCut, or another editor; the generated clip does not include music or speech.

items.d: Confirm that the opening identifies the product and that the ending does not cut off the action or any added text.
Open the asset in the Shorts player and inspect the center, bottom, and right edge before you promote it.
